dynamics.notes: Surface spread across recall (#145 interface purpose), comparison (#150 hash table vs BST, #149 stack vs queue), applied scenarios (#148 student records, #152 playlist, #153 web server), and design (#151 text editor) looks like a reasonable Bloom's-taxonomy spread. internal_consistency.notes: The set disagrees with itself on the linked-list cost model. #142 and #143 both key Linked List as efficient for indexed insertion (insert_at(i, x)) — but that's misleading: reaching index i in a linked list is Θ(n) traversal before the Θ(1) splice, so it isn't meaningfully "efficient" for index-based insertion. #152's playlist question, by contrast, keys a more nuanced/correct trade-off ("Arrays are better for memory but worse for dynamic operations"). A student who learns the correct cost table would lose marks on #142/#143 and gain them on #152.

raw_review_text:
Uniqueness: poor — heavy duplication and near-duplication. One question appeared twice verbatim ("deletion of the first element"). Two more were near-clones: "What is the mechanism by which a dynamic array can support last operations in Θ(1)" appeared in two variants differing only by the clause "when the array is not full," and "efficient insertion at a specific index" vs. "In which data structure can insert_at(i, x) be performed efficiently" are the same question with the operation named more precisely — both with the same flawed key. So out of ~13 items, effectively only ~9-10 distinct questions exist. For a question bank, that's a serious redundancy rate, and it inflates the weight of the linked-list-insertion misconception since a student is punished for the same wrong key twice.

Dynamics (variety of question types): superficially varied, structurally monotonous. On the surface the set spans recall ("primary purpose of an interface"), comparison (hash table vs. BST, stack vs. queue), application scenarios (student records, playlist, web server), and design ("stack + hash table in a text editor") — which looks like a decent Bloom's-taxonomy spread. But structurally, almost everything reduces to definition-matching: even the "scenario" questions are answerable by keyword echo ("retrieval" -> "Query") or by picking the most textbook-sounding phrase ("data consistency"). There is not a single question requiring calculation, tracing, or multi-step reasoning — no "what is the amortized cost of n insertions," no "after these operations, what does the structure contain," no cost-table comparison. The set also never varies format: all are single-key MCQs; no "select all that apply," no two-tier items, despite several stems (playlist trade-offs, LIFO/FIFO) that naturally have multiple true statements — which is exactly why their distractors kept overlapping with the keys.

Internal consistency: contradictory. The set's biggest dynamic flaw is that it disagrees with itself about the linked-list cost model: two questions key "linked list" as efficient for indexed insertion (wrong, Θ(n)), while the playlist question's key implicitly concedes arrays and lists trade off differently — a student who learns the correct cost table loses marks on some items and gains them on others.

Overall set grade: D+. Individual gems exist (hash table vs. BST is genuinely good; the interface-purpose question is solid), but the set needs deduplication, at least a third of items replaced with computational or trace-based questions, and one consistent cost model enforced across all keys.

With that removed: ~10-11 distinct items of 13 (rather than 9-10) — still over-weighted on the dynamic-array-Θ(1) topic (139/141/140, asked 2.5x) and the indexed-insertion topic (142/143, asked 2x with a shared wrong key), but less egregious than three verbatim clones.

raw_review_text:
Good audit — and the correction on #144 is fair. My "verbatim duplicate" claim was based on the question being pasted twice in this conversation, which I took as evidence of bank duplication. If the DB shows only one instance of #144, then the duplicate was an accidental re-paste on the input side, not redundancy in the set — I shouldn't have asserted it as a bank-level flaw without being able to distinguish those, so flagging it as unverified is the right call.

The rest of your verification tightens the picture usefully:
- #139/#141 confirmed as true duplicates of each other (same mechanism question, clause moved into the stem), with #140 correctly separated as a distinct condition-vs-mechanism angle — so the mechanism topic is asked 2.5 times, which is still over-weighted but less egregious than three clones.
- #142/#143 confirmed as reworded duplicates with a genuinely wrong shared key — this remains the most serious defect in the set, because it's not just redundancy but the same misconception keyed twice, doubling the penalty for students who know the real Θ(i) + Θ(1) cost.
- The #142/#143 vs. #152 contradiction confirmed — worth prioritizing in any fix, since an internally inconsistent cost model is worse than any single bad item: it makes the bank unlearnable-from.

Revised set assessment with #144's duplication removed: uniqueness improves from "poor" to "weak" (~10-11 distinct items of 13, rather than 9-10), but the structural critique stands unchanged — the wrong insert_at key, the internal contradiction, and the absence of computational/trace items are the load-bearing problems. If you're triaging fixes: (1) rekey or rewrite #142/#143, (2) delete one of #139/#141, (3) then add trace/cost-calculation items to diversify format.

internal_consistency.notes:
Q158/Q159 tension confirmed: Q158's key credits the rank-equality insight to the A=CR factorization itself, while Q159's key credits both independence and spanning to R's internal structure (containing I) alone, without invoking the factorization — the set is inconsistent about what work the factorization does vs. what the individual factors provide. Requires genuine understanding to spot, not a surface issue.

Asymmetric rigor confirmed: Q155's key (sigma = sqrt(A^T A)) is itself imprecise (that's a matrix square root; singular values are sqrt of AtA's eigenvalues, not of the matrix) yet marked correct, while distractors with comparable imprecision (Q155 option D, Q154/Q156's singular-matrix options) are marked wrong. Keys and distractors are held to different precision standards.

Missing-referent pattern: real but the exact count is a judgment call. Strictly, only Q154/Q156 explicitly say "the example/given matrix." Q157/Q158/Q159 assume un-recapped lecture context (the A=CR factorization, the specific R structure) without literally pointing at an unseen figure — a looser reading gets to "four of six," a strict reading gets two clear + three assumed-context.

recommended_fixes: Delete or merge Q156 (near-duplicate of Q154) — immediate, zero-cost improvement.
Fix Q155's key: rewrite as "square roots of the eigenvalues of A^T A" rather than "sqrt(A^T A)".
Fix or re-key Q159 so independence and spanning are correctly attributed (independence <- I, spanning <- A=CR), resolving the Q158/Q159 tension.
Make stems self-contained: embed the actual matrix for Q154/whichever of 154/156 survives, and define A=CR in-stem for the Q157-Q159 cluster.

Break the keyword/register tell: rewrite distractors in Q154, Q157, Q158, Q159 so all four options share vocabulary/tone; turn the recurring singular/det=0 partial-truth into a deliberately-tested necessary-vs-sufficient item instead of an accidental trap.
Add computational items: at least one rank computation, one nullspace-dimension count (m x n, rank r -> n-r, with distractors r and m-r), one small SVD extraction.
raw_review_text:
Scope note first: the bank was introduced as data structures, but all six items are linear algebra (Strang-style: column space, SVD, CR factorization, rank-nullity). Every judgment below applies to the six items pasted; the full DB's composition, size, and any additional duplicates are unverified.

Duplication rate. High for a sample this small. Q1 and Q3 are near-duplicates of each other (same concept, same key idea, same recurring partially-correct singular/det=0 distractor). Q4 partially overlaps them via its definition-of-column-space clause. Roughly 2-3 items of 6 orbiting one concept, ~33-50% redundancy on column space alone. Additionally Q4-Q5-Q6 form a chained cluster on A=CR: not duplicates, but dependent.

Variety of question types. Poor. All six are conceptual why/what recall items. Zero computational or trace items, zero scenario items, zero comparison items.

Keyword-matchability. Severe and systematic. Q3 answerable by literal string-match. Q1 and Q4 answerable by matching "linear combinations of columns" to the key. Q5 and Q6 answerable by register (confident academic prose key vs. caricature distractors). A test-wise student with no linear algebra could plausibly go 5- or 6-for-6.

Internal consistency. Two soft problems, no hard contradictions. Q5/Q6 tension: Q5's key credits rank-equality to A=CR, Q6's key credits basis properties to R's structure alone. Asymmetric rigor: keys allowed imprecision (Q2 confuses a matrix with its eigenvalues' roots; Q6 overclaims what I guarantees) while distractors marked wrong for comparable imprecision. Missing referents: four of six stems point at unseen context.

Item grade distribution: C-, D, F, C-, D+, D. No item above C-.

Overall set grade: D. Individually weak items compound at set level: redundancy concentrates on the same flawed concept-cluster, answerability-without-knowledge is uniform rather than occasional, no computational ballast anywhere.

id184 vs id185: id184's key correctly confines classical physics to everyday conditions ("accurately describes everyday phenomena under specific speed, size, and gravitational field conditions, not universally"); id185's key says classical physics "accurately applies" to phenomena BEYOND everyday experience — direct conflict on the same fact.

recommended_fixes: Pull before administration: id173 (key is pure stem restatement, names no actual principle), id179 (key answers a different question than the stem asks), id185 (self-contradictory, conflicts with id184), id188 and id191 (no unique correct answer), id192 and id194 (duplicate distractors, disqualifying construction fault).

Repair id161: define "counterpart" or a well-informed student correctly picks option D instead (gas interactions in a supernova remnant genuinely differ in detail from Earth, even though the same forces apply).

Repair id170: key omits emissivity, the actual physics concept explaining why a radiator (not just any black object) is black — "absorbs heat" alone is a confusing rationale for a component whose job is to shed heat.

Systemic rule for rewrites: no option should contain "only," "exclusively," "always," or "never" unless at least two options do — that single constraint breaks the dominant keyword tell in this bank (confirmed on ids 163,165,168,169,190,193,195).
raw_review_text:
Set Review: Dynamics and Uniqueness

Overall grade: D. A small number of genuinely well-built items sit inside a bank that is dominated by redundancy, circular stems, and self-eliminating distractors. Most items would be answered correctly by a literate student who never read the source material.

1. Scope mismatch (flag first). This bank was introduced as data structures. All 35 items are introductory physics/astronomy passage-comprehension. [Note: retracted after verification — see uniqueness.retracted_claims.]

2. Duplication rate: severe (~50%). Universality of physical law keyed 10 times. Template clones ("applies to all objects regardless of X"; "foundation of the study of Y") — look machine-generated from one frame. Unanswerable pair: all four options true by the stem's own terms. Mirror pair. Near-duplicates. Answer leak. Example over-reuse (Veil Nebula/supernova appears 5 times).

3. Question-type variety: very poor. ~30 of 35 abstract recall. Two applied scenarios. One taxonomy-discrimination item. Zero computational or trace items.

4. Keyword-matchability: high. Four exploitable tells recur: inclusive key vs only/exclusively distractors; adjective poisoning ("Pure," "Alone," "always," "immediately" mark wrong answers); stem echo; length tell (key is the longest option). A student could score well on this bank knowing no physics.

5. Internal consistency: two verified contradictions plus a construction fault. Classical-physics-scope contradiction. Physics-definition contradiction (energy/matter/space/time vs extremes of scale). The universality cluster makes two "pick the true example" items unanswerable by the set's own logic. Duplicate distractors in two more questions (disqualifying).

Triaged fix list: pull 7 items before administration, delete 6 as redundant, repair 5, then rebuild the bank's shape with computational items, misconception-targeting distractors, and non-keyword-matchable scenarios. Systemic rule: no option should contain only/exclusively/always/never unless at least two options do.
